candidates.title: Between Periods
candidates.pitch: It is intermission and the rink is a wreck: skate grooves, divots, and one seeded mishap such as a shower of hats or a split water tank. The visitor steers a small ice-resurfacing machine on a 2D rink, laying shave, wash and squeegee passes so that every scar is covered before the buzzer while a limited water tank empties. The finished sheet gleams, and the result becomes a polished postcard of your own lap pattern that friends can race as a ghost via the link.
candidates.whyNow: The 2026-27 hockey season is underway (opened Sept. 29, 2026), so rink lore is in the air, but the mechanic (coverage routing under a turning-radius limit, with a daily rink) works all season and beyond.

research.summary: Two threads shape the design. First, the real machine does a fixed sequence on each pass (shave a thin layer, collect shavings, spray, vacuum dirty water, lay clean water, squeegee smooth), which gives three layered passes and a water budget as natural mechanics, and its all-wheel steering was cut to front-wheel steering because it kept wedging against the boards, which justifies a turning-radius limit that makes routing a real puzzle. The history and mechanism sources are single search entries with blended summaries, so they stay unverified and the page cites them as reported. Second, the shareable-seed craft: a seed is one value that reproduces the same generated world, daily puzzles commonly derive the day's puzzle from the UTC date and share results as a spoiler-light grid, and state can be packed compactly into a URL fragment. The season-start date is confirmed by two separate headlines. Sources are about the concept only; no player or team data is used.

facts.claim: The 2026-27 NHL regular season opened on Sept. 29, 2026 with Florida at Carolina and Montreal at Toronto among the opening-night games (as seen in headlines on 2026-10-12).
A seed is a single starting value that makes a procedurally generated world reproducible, so the same seed on the same code version gives the same world.
As reported by a mechanism explainer, an ice resurfacing pass shaves the surface, collects the shavings, rinses, then lays clean water and squeegees it smooth.
As reported by a history article, the first resurfacing machine dates to 1949 and replaced a multi-person hand process.
A small daily-games site states that its puzzle is derived from the UTC date and its stats live only in local storage.

inspirations: daily golf and daily crossword share cards

design.coreLoop: Each day's rink (seeded from the date, or from a seed in the URL hash) has a wear map of grooves and divots plus one mishap hazard. The player drives a machine with a real turning radius and a finite water tank, laying a wide three-stage swath; they plan lanes to cover every scar with minimal overlap and refill at the tank door. The score rewards clean coverage, little overlap, and speed against the intermission clock, and retries expose a better lane plan each time, from lawn-mower stripes to spirals that save turns.
sophisticationHooks: Hash-reconstructed world: #seed plus an optional quantized, delta-coded path of a few hundred bytes lets a friend load the identical rink and race your ghost.
Hero moment: a wet-ice sheen stripe follows the machine across the rink and dries to a high-gloss finish, with a soft three-note intermission chime from WebAudio that starts muted.
Spoiler-safe share postcard drawn on canvas: your lap pattern rendered as a gleaming print with grade, no rink layout needed to read it, plus a copy-text emoji strip.
Daily mishap table plus an optional dim-hall mode where only a headlamp pool reveals scars (the blind variant), marked on the card with a moon.
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: seeded rink generator, steering model with turning radius, coverage mask on an offscreen canvas, water tank and refill, scoring, ghost recording and playback, URL hash read/write, canvas share card, keyboard and touch steering, light and dark, reduced motion, making-of panel. Cut: multiple machine models, online leaderboards, music, any real team or player data.
risks: The maker's trademarked name must not appear on the page; use the generic term ice resurfacer.
Mechanism and history facts are unverified search snippets; the page shows them as 'as of 2026-10-12, per the cited article' or omits them.
Touch steering at 360px needs a drag-to-aim scheme with 44px targets; mitigate with a tilt-free pointer-follow mode.
Ghost path in the URL must stay short: quantize to a coarse grid and cap at a few seconds of samples per segment.
Daily seed uses UTC date so everyone shares one rink; the page states this.

candidates.title: Smudged Memos
candidates.pitch: A clerk at an invented Bureau of Misplaced Things receives sealed memos in cipher, each one an absurd grievance built from a hand-written grammar, with a spilled-tea mishap blotting some letters. The visitor works a bench of frequency charts, repeat finders, shift wheels and crib-dragging to crack it, without being told which cipher family it is. Then they can forge a memo of their own from the grammar, pick a cipher and a blot level, and send the link, which carries a sealed envelope that only the recipient can open.
candidates.whyNow: Timeless: a daily memo gives a reason to return and the forge-and-send path makes the page spread person to person; autumn paperwork humor needs no news hook.

research.summary: Real cryptanalysis supplies the depth: repeated ciphertext fragments of three or more letters hint at the key length of a polyalphabetic cipher (Kasiski), the index of coincidence compares letter-pairing odds against English-like text to test key lengths, and once the length is known each column falls to frequency analysis. That gives a legitimate toolkit the player can use, and it scales from a shift cipher to a short keyword cipher. On the sharing side, daily puzzles commonly use a result grid or card that hides the answer, a pattern the sources describe for Wordle-style games. Putting state in the URL fragment is practical, and a source notes that anyone holding the link can read it, so the sealed memo is deliberately a puzzle, not a secret. All memo text is generated from a bundled grammar of invented, harmless office grievances; nothing is user-typed free text.

facts.claim: Repeated ciphertext fragments of length three or more, and the distances between them, are used (Kasiski examination) to estimate the key length of a Vigenere-style cipher.
Once the key length is known, each column of a Vigenere ciphertext is a shifted-alphabet sample solvable by frequency analysis.
Wordle-style daily puzzles share results as a colored-square summary so the answer is not revealed to other players.
As reported by a small daily-games site, puzzles can be derived from the UTC date and stats kept only in the browser's local storage.
As reported by a developer article, data stored in a URL fragment is readable by anyone who has the link unless encrypted.

design.coreLoop: Open the day's sealed memo, a screen of ciphered text with a few tea-blotted letters. Use the bench to gather evidence (letter frequencies, repeat spacing, a shift wheel, trial crib words slid along the text) and pencil letters in; each hint spends from a small ink budget. Cracking it reveals a short absurd memo and a postmark card; then the forge lets the player compose a new memo from the grammar and send it. Variety comes from the cipher family (shift, keyword substitution, short Vigenere, rail fence) staying hidden until identified.
sophisticationHooks: A real cipher bench: frequency histogram against expected English, Kasiski-style repeat finder, draggable shift wheel, crib drag, all computed client-side on a bundled word list.
Blind identification: the cipher family is undisclosed, and the bench's evidence panels (flat histogram, repeat spacing) are how the player deduces it.
Forge and send: grammar-slot composer, cipher and blot choice, and a hash that reconstructs the exact sealed memo, shown to the recipient as a postmarked envelope with an opening animation.
Spoiler-safe wax-seal share card: stamp, ink used, and blot count only, never the plaintext or the cipher family, drawn on canvas and copyable as text.
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: grammar and ~300-word vocabulary of invented office grievances, four cipher implementations with solvers for verification, the bench tools, seeded daily memo, forge composer, hash encode/decode, envelope and seal rendering, keyboard and touch input, light and dark, reduced motion, making-of panel. Cut: sound, user-typed free text, accounts, streak leaderboards.
risks: Overlaps in category and mechanic with other word-puzzle candidates today; the forge-and-send path and the instrument-like bench are the differentiators.
Index-of-coincidence numbers were not verified; the page computes them from its own corpus and does not quote external values.
Short messages may be ambiguous to crack; mitigate by checking at generation time that each memo is uniquely solvable with the bench tools and has a minimum length.
Because the link carries the memo, all text must come from the bundled grammar to avoid user-authored abuse; no free text input.
Grievance humor must stay about invented objects and offices, never real organizations or people.
